summary.title: Hashing
summary.one_liner: An interactive, visual introduction to hash functions: how to judge their quality with collisions, distribution grids and the avalanche effect, how hash maps use them, and why seeding defends against manufactured collisions (HashDoS).
takeaways: A good hash function is deterministic, maps inputs to a bounded range, and spreads outputs uniformly so collisions are rare.
The avalanche effect measures how many output bits flip when one input bit changes; a good function flips about 50%.
A hash map uses a hash function to pick a bucket, then scans that bucket for the key; uniform hashes keep buckets short and operations fast.
Attackers can find many colliding inputs for weak hash functions (HashDoS), and a random seed makes collisions unpredictable.
summary.summary: The article starts by defining hash functions as deterministic functions from input (usually a string) to a number in a fixed range, then explains collisions. It evaluates hash functions visually by plotting outputs on grids of 10,000 random strings, sequential numbers and English words, contrasting a good function (TV-static look) with a deliberately bad one that shows striping. It then covers the avalanche effect via bit-flip histograms. Next it builds a simple HashMap class in JavaScript with buckets, set and get methods, and shows that poor distribution slows lookups. Finally it demonstrates manufactured collisions against murmur3, explains how a seed randomises output to mitigate HashDoS, and includes the murmur3 source and further reading.
